papers.title: Time-Varying Bayesian Optimization and Extremum Seekingfor Drift-Tube Linac Tuning at LANSCE
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a promising machine learning approach to accelerator tuning. It has the advantage of being able to incorporate prior information, including simulation and historical data, and explicitly model measurement noise. However, standard implementations can produce large, abrupt parameter updates that are undesirable and potentially unsafe in accelerator operation. They may also spend excessive time exploring less promising regions of the search space. We address these limitations by imposing soft and hard step size limits. We evaluate these methods by adjusting the radio frequency settings of the drift tube linac (DTL) at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE) to maximize the particle count at the end of the linac. We first test the methods in simulation with constant exogenous parameters, then repeat the tests with drifting exogenous parameters. Under drifting conditions, progressively reducing the BO step size limit improved convergence. We also find that an initial BO segment followed by extremum seeking (ES), an approach we call BO-ES, combines BO's use of prior information and sample efficiency with ES's effectiveness in local optimization and drift tracking. Finally, tests on the LANSCE accelerator with BO-ES demonstrate an approximately $25\%$ reduction in losses at the end of the linac across different configurations of historical and simulation data.

papers.title: Residual diffusion for fine-structure enhancement in low-count accelerator-based muon imaging
papers.abstract: Accelerator-based muon imaging combines the penetrating power of high-energy muons with selectable momentum and a controlled beam direction, offering a powerful means of probing internal structures in large, dense and heavily shielded objects. Within a fixed beam-time budget, realizing this potential requires reliable recovery of fine structures from limited muon statistics. We propose an observation-conditioned residual diffusion method with decoupled linear schedules to enhance low-count muon images through iterative restoration guided by the observed image. We evaluate a simplified VSC-24 fuel cask under an idealized 5 GeV parallel muon beam, using 500,000 accepted events per low-count image and 40 million per reference image. Simulation results show improved recovery of structural boundaries and fine details, with the mean peak signal-to-noise ratio increasing from 11.4239 to 22.1719 dB. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion models to make more effective use of limited muon data and broaden the application of accelerator-based muon imaging across scientific and industrial settings.

papers.title: Beam-Driven Active Plasma Dechirper for Energy Stabilization of High-Charge Bunches
papers.abstract: Plasma-based accelerators offer ultrahigh electric field gradients, yet delivering high-charge bunches with simultaneously low energy jitter and narrow energy spread remains a critical challenge. We propose a beam-driven active plasma dechirper integrated with a magnetic chicane to suppress both imperfections. By operating in the blowout regime at low plasma density, the dechirper accommodates a stretched witness bunch, thereby mitigating beam-loading effects and preserving the linear slope of the longitudinal wakefield for precise energy stabilization. Furthermore, a tailored initial energy chirp is introduced to reconcile the disparate optimal plasma lengths required for correcting jitter and spread. Three-dimensional simulations demonstrate that for a 1~GeV, 1~nC electron bunch, this scheme simultaneously reduces the energy jitter and spread from $\pm2$\% and 1\% to $\pm0.05$\% and 0.05\%, respectively, while maintaining nearly 100\% transmission.

papers.title: Brilliance: toward autonomous computational research in particle accelerator physics
papers.abstract: Computational research requires repeated decisions about models, calculations and the interpretation of results. We introduce Brilliance, an agent that combines large language models, reusable physics expertise and numerical simulation to construct and revise investigations in accelerator physics. Starting from a detailed expert-specified request, Brilliance develops an ideal storage-ring lattice meeting the specified emittance ceiling and sampled nonlinear-acceptance criteria after revising optics that fail particle-tracking tests. Further scientist-guided exploration produces a candidate with a natural emittance of 6.51 pm rad and millimeter-scale transverse acceptance, while exposing unresolved momentum-acceptance limitations. Using measured responses from the High Energy Photon Source, Brilliance also performs offline optics calibration consistent with an independent specialist analysis. An expert-module ablation examines how reusable domain knowledge influences research choices and outcomes. Here, we demonstrate a practical route to scientist-agent collaboration in sustained numerical research.
